newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Bank Austria takes over Creditanstalt. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Bank Austria takes over Creditanstalt. [CORRECTED 12:30 GMT]

text.p: Austria ended Europe's longest running privatisation battle on Sunday when it sold flagship bank Creditanstalt to arch-rival Bank Austria, raising the spectre of a major shakeup in the country's banking sector.

"I can tell you that the state's stake in Creditanstalt will go to the highest bidder which is Bank Austria," Chancellor Franz Vranitzky told reporters after marathon talks between coalition leaders of his Social Democratic Party and the conservative People's Party.
The conservatives had opposed the sale of Creditanstalt to Bank Austria, which is indirectly controlled by the Social Democrat-dominated City of Vienna.

The two parties struck a last-ditch deal which effectively ensures the privatisation of Bank Austria with the bank guaranteeing a buyout of Creditanstalt's small shareholders -- two key conservative demands.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima told reporters after an 11-hour round of closed-door talks that Bank Austria had offered a total of 17.2 billion schillings ($1.55 billion) for the state's 70 percent voting stake in Creditanstalt.

Bank Austria also offered to buy out Creditanstalt's small shareholders, offering them a premium of about two schillings ($0.180) on ordinary voting shares, which on Friday closed at 720.50 schillings ($64.97) in Vienna.
Klima said he would put his signature on the sale contract on Sunday. "The transaction will be closed immediately, I will go to my office right now and sign the contract," he said.
Vranitzky said Bank Austria would be taken out of public control step by step.

According to the agreement, the state's 19 percent stake in the market leader would be floated immediately, while the 45 percent stake held by the City of Vienna's Anteilsverwaltung Zentralsparkasse (AVZ) foundation would be cut to below 20 percent within seven (corrects from five) years.
The reduction of AVZ's stake would be achieved through a series of capital increases in which the foundation would not take part, Klima said.
Conservative leader Wolfgang Schuessel said Creditanstalt would remain an independent bank for at least five years.

The two banks will have combined assets of about 14 billion schillings ($1.26 billion) and control a major part of Austria's retail and wholesale banking market. The two banks also have wide-ranging interests in the country's key industries.

A Bank Austria spokesman told Reuters the bank would hold a news conference on Sunday at 1 p.m. (1200 GMT) to outline its strategy for Creditanstalt, once banker to the imperial Habsburg family of Austro-Hungarian emperors.
There was no immediate statement from an international consortium of industrial and financial interests led by insurer EA-Generali, which had submitted a rival bid. ($1=11.09 Schilling)
